Collision Report — i2m Futures Innovation

Circular Materials for Resilient Cities

Different perspectives test a cross-industry material loop for resilient cities.

MANN+HUMMEL
Fixed challenge

How might we build climate resilient cities?

Step 01 / 05

Challenge Framing

A cross-industry material loop tested against urban resilience needs.

Job-to-be-Done

When manufacturers generate recoverable offcuts and urban suppliers need dependable materials, they need a traceable way to collect, qualify and route each stream into suitable products, so they can reduce waste and test whether local supply becomes more resilient.

Top 3 Pains
  • Usable production offcuts are dispersed across companies and often lack the data needed for a new application.
  • Collection, sorting, testing and transport have no clear owner across industries.
  • Product performance, regulatory fit, climate impact and total delivered cost remain unproven.
Top 3 Gains
  • Qualified secondary materials can be matched to suitable urban products instead of being discarded.
  • A documented return route links producers, a central hub and receiving industries.
  • Transparent quality, cost and impact data support a decision on whether to scale the loop.
Step 02 / 05

Expert Panel

Distinct perspectives selected to challenge the concept.

The panel tests city resilience through climate outcomes, urban ecology, essential-service reliability, economics, governance and inclusion. These are simulated analytical lenses, not the named individuals’ stated views on this proposal.

Bold Proposal

Create a cross-industry compact with named owners for collection, qualification, routing and city procurement.

Looks for significant customer pain points, large market opportunities, and a credible path to differentiation. Balances ambition with realism by assessing strategic fit, competitive advantage, unique assets, technology leverage, partnerships, and long-term business potential. Accepts uncertainty in the early stages and avoids asking for excessive proof before the opportunity has been properly explored.

Provocation

Step 03 / 05

The Collision Meeting

Illustrative dialogue between the selected perspectives.

WM
William McDonough → opens the material-loop proposal

A return hub only works if textile offcuts are sorted by composition and designed for a useful next cycle. Otherwise we merely relocate waste.

JS
Julian Simon → responds to William McDonough

I agree on quality, but do not lock every qualified fiber into acoustic panels. Let suitable industries compete so we learn where each stream creates value.

GT
Greta Thunberg → challenges Julian Simon

Then measure transport, processing energy and displaced virgin material for each route. A longer journey could erase the claimed climate benefit.

MS
Michael Shellenberger → responds to Greta Thunberg

That comparison also needs reliable volume and specification. An acoustic manufacturer cannot plan around a stream that changes every week.

KO
Kate Orff → responds to Michael Shellenberger

Start with one suitable city-building application. Qualify the textile batch for acoustic performance, fire safety and maintenance before choosing the design.

DF
Diana Furchtgott-Roth → challenges Kate Orff

Include collection, sorting, testing and rejected batches in the delivered cost. A promising prototype does not prove an affordable supply system.

WG
Wawa Gatheru → responds to Diana Furchtgott-Roth

Cost is not only financial. Where will sorting and transport happen, and will the workers and neighboring communities share the benefits?

AD
Ani Dasgupta → builds on Wawa Gatheru

Put those choices into a chain with named owners: producer, hub, qualifier, buyer and city. Every handoff needs a quality gate and accountability.

CV
Charles Vaillant → challenges Ani Dasgupta

That is a plausible system, but who is the paying customer: the textile producer, the acoustic maker or the city buyer? Interview all three before deciding who should own the hub.

Step 04 / 05

Collision Combinations

Three ways to turn material recovery into a testable cross-industry system.

Combination

Qualified Cross-Industry Routing

Combine McDonough’s material-cycle test with Simon’s openness to alternatives: grade textile offcuts, then route qualified batches to acoustic products or other verified uses rather than assuming one destination.

Combination

Climate Benefit at Full Cost

Combine Thunberg’s outcome test with Furchtgott-Roth’s cost test and Shellenberger’s supply test: compare emissions, transport, accepted yield, reliable volume and delivered price against the current route.

Combination

Accountable Hub With Shared Value

Combine Dasgupta’s governance, Gatheru’s community lens and Vaillant’s customer test: name the hub owner and paying buyer, then check worker and neighborhood impacts before scaling.

Step 05 / 05

The Final Concept

A shared return hub and three tests before any scale-up decision.

Final Concept

Cross-Industry Materials Loop

A proposed reverse-logistics system sends recoverable production scrap back to a shared central hub. The hub records origin, sorts and qualifies each stream, then routes it to a suitable receiving industry. For example, textile offcuts could supply acoustic-product manufacturers if safety and performance requirements are met. Partners would track quantities, specifications, destinations and later take-back. Its contribution to city resilience, climate outcomes and business value remains to be tested.

Why It Is Non-Obvious

The proposal joins reverse logistics, material qualification and demand across industries rather than recycling one waste stream in isolation. The difficult step is matching variable scrap to a buyer’s specification at a viable delivered cost. A central hub has value only if it solves that coordination problem and improves outcomes compared with existing routes.

3 First Experiment Steps · ≤ 6 weeks
1

Map one textile offcut stream and one potential acoustic-product buyer. Document composition, available volume, current disposal route, product requirements and named owners; identify one stream and one buyer willing to test it.

2

Test a representative sample against the buyer’s acoustic, fire-safety and material requirements. Record accepted yield, rejected material and the full collection-to-delivery cost; proceed only if the buyer’s minimum criteria are met.

3

Trial one small return route through the hub or a partner site. Track quantity, quality, transport, handling cost and an impact estimate against the current route; agree a documented go, redirect or stop decision with the producer and buyer.
